slides.texte_overlay:
Things that make you
surprisingly good at
listening to her
Put your phone face down, then in your pocket. When she starts telling you something, give her your full attention. It's the simplest way to show that what she says matters to you.
Ask about feelings, not just facts. Not only "What happened next?" but "How did that feel?" People feel truly heard when you care about their experience, not just the story.
Don't jump straight to fixing it. Sometimes she just wants to vent. Ask "Do you want advice or do you just want me to listen?" It's one of the kindest questions you can ask.
Remember the details and bring them back. Her colleague's name, the exam date, the trip she's planning. Following up days later shows you were really listening.
Before: half listening, waiting for my turn to talk. After: five minutes a day of history, art or science, a calmer head, and real curiosity about her stories.
slides.texte_sophia: Before: half listening, waiting for my turn. After: five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. A calmer head and real curiosity about her stories.

slides.texte_overlay: Reflect back what you heard. "So you felt left out because they didn't ask you?" It shows you understood, and it lets her correct you if you missed something.
Let silence happen after she shares something big. Don't rush to fill it. A quiet moment and a hand on her shoulder often says more than any perfect answer.
